name: Amira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for Marlow Builders, a small firm in a seaside town. We do loft conversions and back extensions, mostly for families who can't afford to move so they build up instead. Right now we're turning a loft on Harbour Road into a bedroom for two teenage boys. I'm there at half seven, I set out the new floor joists, frame the dormer window, and keep the two young carpenters on my crew busy. At lunch I'm on my phone, putting the client's rough sketch into an AI app so it gives them a 3D picture of their new room by the evening.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a family climbs the new stairs for the first time. Last month a mum on Pier Street just stood there and said, we've got a whole extra floor. What wears me out is that I do half the design and the customer talking, and I'm still paid like a carpenter on a lower rate. Marlow's is one of only three builders in town, so I can't exactly shop around. My husband Karim's a mechanic, and after our wedding last year we've got almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a great tool, just not magic. I'd probably post one of my 3D drawings and say, this is what it's good for, the rest was hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the tools I already use stay useful, and I keep being the one at Marlow's who can show clients a picture before we start. That's worth something, even if I'm not paid for it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day, and I'd start charging for the design side. A few homeowners have asked me to do drawings for jobs Marlow's isn't doing. Maybe two a month on weekends, a couple of hundred each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite content, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does your boss know how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He knows I do the pictures, he thinks it's clever. I don't think he knows it also prices half our jobs. He's old school. He just likes that customers sign faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what are you working towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own firm. Small, family-run, honest prices. Me doing the design and the frame, Karim's cousin doing the plastering. I want my children one day to see their mum's name on a van.

S0.say: I'd say it's still a great tool, just not magic. I'd post one of my 3D drawings and say this is what it's good for and the rest was hype.
S0.think: The tools I already use stay useful, and I keep being the one who can show clients a picture before we start. That's worth something, even if I'm not paid for it yet.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and starts charging for design work on weekends, about two jobs a month at a couple of hundred each. Keeps working as lead carpenter at Marlow's.
S0.quote: I want my children one day to see their mum's name on a van.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is ambitious and entrepreneurial, using AI to do design and pricing her old-school boss doesn't fully see. Her goal of a family-run firm fits her traditional values. Savings are thin after her wedding, but she has a clear side income in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on with it. The people who learn the tools will do well, and that's fair. You can't stop progress by complaining about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Lofts and extensions are fiddly, every house is different, and I can already do the design and pricing with AI. If robots do the heavy lifting, I can run more jobs with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the design side into a proper business, drawings and project plans for homeowners. I'd get a laser scanner on finance, about forty a month, so I can measure a loft in ten minutes. And I'd learn every new tool that comes along, the day it comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like the door's opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might buy a scanner. On almost no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On finance, yes. It's a risk, but it pays for itself in two or three jobs. Karim was nervous, but I showed him the sums and he agreed, as long as it's the only one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gets hurt in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who won't learn. I feel for them, but I'm not sure the government should carry them. Their families, their churches, the firms that trained them, that's where help should come from. And apprenticeships, retraining on the job.

S1.say: I'd say get on with it: people who learn the tools will do well, and that's fair. You can't stop progress by complaining about it.
S1.think: It's good for me, because lofts are fiddly and I already do design and pricing with AI. If robots do the heavy lifting, I can run more jobs with fewer people.
S1.do: Grows her weekend design work into a proper business and buys a laser scanner on finance at about 40 a month. Learns every new tool the day it comes out.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a door opening.
S1.quote: You can't stop progress by complaining about it.
S1.fieldNote: Amira sees steady change as an opening and would take a small financed risk with her husband's agreement. Her view of who should help displaced workers, family, church and firms rather than government, fits her outlook. She is confident but checks the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and it's fast, but there's opportunity in it for people who move quickly. I'd also say look after your family first, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast even for me. If the robot can do the design too, my edge goes. And with almost no savings and a scanner on finance, one bad month and we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to become the person who organises the robots for homeowners: you want a loft, I bring the machine, I check the work, I talk to the family. I'd cut back hard at home, no holidays, no eating out. And Karim and I would lean on his parents if we had to, they've offered before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be pushing hard, but I'd feel the pressure every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money worries you more than the robots. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can learn anything new in a week. I can't make money appear. Without a cushion, you can't afford to be the first one to try something, and that's my whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan would say, God gives you two hands for a reason. She'd tell me to keep working and stop worrying. She'd probably feed me as well. Sunday lunch at hers is the one thing I wouldn't cut.

S2.say: I'd say it's huge and fast, but there's opportunity for people who move quickly. I'd also say look after your family first, because nobody else will.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me: if the robot can design too, my edge goes. With almost no savings and a scanner on finance, one bad month and we're in trouble.
S2.do: Sets herself up as the person who brings and checks robots for homeowners' loft jobs and handles the family. Cuts household spending hard and leans on her husband's parents if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, pushing hard but feeling the pressure every day.
S2.quote: Without a cushion, you can't afford to be the first one to try something, and that's my whole plan.
S2.fieldNote: Even adaptive and confident, Amira finds her thin savings are the real limit in the fast picture. She would still move first, positioning herself to manage robots for families. Family, faith and Sunday lunch at her grandmother's are her anchors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. Learn the machines, build your name, don't wait for someone else to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is a real chance for me. Enough time to get my own firm going before it fully lands, and to be the one using the robots rather than replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and grow the weekend design work, saving every pound of it towards a van and insurance. By year two I'd want regular clients and a few months of money in the bank. Then I'd start hiring robot kit for the heavy jobs as soon as it's on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave Marlow's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I've got six months of work booked and three months of money saved. Not before. Mr Marlow's been good to me, I'd give him proper notice and maybe even send him jobs I can't take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Karim's garage started going under, maybe. Cars will change too. Then we'd need my wage steady and I'd hold off. Family comes before the plan.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. Learn the machines, build your name and don't wait for someone else to save you.
S3.think: Five years is a real chance for me to get my own firm going before it lands and be the one using robots rather than replaced by them.
S3.do: Keeps her job and grows weekend design work, saving it all towards a van and insurance. Aims for regular clients and a few months saved by year two, then hires robot kit for heavy work as soon as it is offered.
S3.fieldNote: Amira's five-year plan is staged and cautious about cash, with clear conditions before she leaves her job. She is loyal to her current boss. The one thing that would stop her is her husband's work faltering, showing family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift, ten years to get ready. Anyone young who doesn't use it, that's on them. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite excited. Ten years is enough to build a proper family firm and have it running with machines before most people have started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a couple of years, then leave Marlow's around year three and start my own firm doing lofts and extensions. I'd put money into the scanner, a van, and later a robot framer when they're affordable. Karim might even join me on the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your firm look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Me, Karim, maybe two people from the town, and a couple of machines doing the heavy work. Families still want someone they trust in their house. The robot can lift the joists, but it won't sit at the kitchen table with the mum and work out where the cot goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Anything that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that big companies come in with robot crews and cheap prices and squeeze small firms out. But that's business, you compete. People round here still like buying local.

S4.say: I'd say ten years to get ready is a gift, and young people who don't use it have only themselves to blame. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.
S4.think: I'd be quite excited. Ten years is enough to build a proper family firm and have it running with machines before most people have started.
S4.do: Saves for a couple of years, then leaves Marlow's around year three to start her own loft and extension firm. Invests in a scanner, a van and later a robot framer, possibly bringing her husband into the business.
S4.quote: The robot can lift the joists, but it won't sit at the kitchen table with the mum and work out where the cot goes.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Amira's free-market optimism is at its strongest: her only worry is competition, which she accepts as fair. She sees her edge as trust and human contact in people's homes. Her plan blends family business and automation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no money to start anything and no time to save. What would help is small loans for tradespeople starting up, and keeping the paperwork simple so a small firm can actually use the new machines. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small firms and families. The robots will be owned by someone. I'd rather it's thousands of little family firms than three giant companies. That's the version I'd fight for.

headlineQuote: I'd rather it's thousands of little family firms than three giant companies.
portrait: Amira is a 27-year-old lead carpenter for a small builder doing loft conversions in a seaside town, married to Karim, a mechanic, with almost no savings after their wedding. She uses AI every day to design and price jobs and dreams of her own family-run firm. She is calm, even excited, in the slower pictures and plans to buy a scanner and later a robot framer, but AGI in two years makes her anxious because her thin cushion stops her moving first. Across all the pictures she relies on family and faith, prefers fair starts to handouts, and bets that people will always want someone they trust in their home.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no money to start anything and no time to save.
whatWouldHelp: Small start-up loans for tradespeople and simple paperwork so small firms can use the new machines, a fair start rather than handouts.
